findings.title: New abstract order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider.order() is added as an abstract method with no default. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider that compiled against the old interface will fail with AbstractMethodError / NoSuchMethodError at runtime and fail to compile. For backward compatibility this should be a default method (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }).

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns unrelated KeyStore provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is typically SUN/JKS, not BouncyCastle. Callers expect a BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider and use it for BC-specific algorithms and BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER logic. Returning an arbitrary JCA provider is misleading and will cause NoSuchAlgorithm/NoSuchProvider failures or wrong algorithm behavior when the authz provider is selected.

findings.title: First-init-wins + ordering can lock server to weak authz provider
findings.body: CryptoIntegration.init() is a no-op once cryptoProvider is set. AuthzClient.create() calls init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). If an authz-client operation runs first in a VM that later hosts the server, the low-priority AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100, most methods throw UnsupportedOperationException) becomes the global provider and full providers (order 200) are never adopted. Conversely standalone authz-client use gets a provider where signature/keyfactory/cert operations all throw. Initialization order therefore silently determines correctness.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion silently truncates/pads negative or oversized integers
findings.body: integerToBytes() converts BigInteger r/s to fixed length by truncating leading bytes or zero-padding with no range check. A negative BigInteger (from new BigInteger(bytes) interpreting high-bit as sign) or a value >= 2^(8*qLength) is silently wrapped instead of rejected. DER signatures must have 0 < r,s < n; accepting/rewriting out-of-range values breaks verification semantics and can hide malformed/forged signatures.

findings.title: Signed BigInteger parsing of DER INTEGER
findings.body: ASN1Decoder.readInteger() uses new BigInteger(bytes), which interprets bytes as two's-complement signed. DER INTEGERs for ECDSA r/s are unsigned and use a leading zero for the high-bit case. A malicious encoding without the leading zero becomes negative instead of being rejected, and flows into integerToBytes() above. It should use new BigInteger(1, bytes) plus explicit range validation.

findings.title: Test uses P-256 key for ES384/ES512 so curve coverage is fake
findings.body: The test fixture generates one KeyPair with KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair(), which defaults to secp256r1/P-256. testES384 and testES512 then sign with that P-256 key but convert with algorithm.getSignatureLength() of 96/132. The conversion round-trip rsConcat->DER->rsConcat holds for any length due to pad/truncate logic, so the tests pass without ever exercising real P-384/P-521 keys, DER sizes, or JCA verification.

findings.title: Dead discarded ASN1Encoder writes
findings.body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER() contains two lines ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and ...write(sBigInteger) whose results are discarded immediately before building the real sequence. They are dead code left over from development and should be removed to avoid confusion about encoding.

findings.title: Crypto init uses class loader instead of context class loader
findings.body: AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). ServiceLoader detection in modular, OSGi, shaded-client, or app-server environments typically needs the thread context class loader. Using the defining loader can fail to discover the Default/Elytron/FIPS provider or discover a different set than the rest of Keycloak, making provider selection environment-dependent.
